analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose the fees they receive from drugmakers.
analysis.headline: The PBM fee-disclosure bill never got a hearing or vote, dying in committee with zero cosponsors when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices for Medicare drug plans, Medicare Advantage plans, and ACA marketplace plans — to report to Medicare and to health plans exactly how much money they take in from drug manufacturers, broken down by type, and how much of that money is passed back to the plans. It would also require the agency that runs Medicare to publish a yearly summary of what those reports show, starting with plan years in 2027. It is a transparency bill: it requires disclosure, but does not cap prices or ban any PBM practice.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in Medicare drug plans, Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage, and ACA marketplace plans, along with the employers and plans that hire PBMs, would gain visibility into how much money PBMs collect from manufacturers in fees and rebates and how much actually flows back to the plan. That information could later support regulation or bargaining over how drug dollars are divided.

how_it_helps.text: Requires PBMs and any affiliated price negotiators or group purchasers to report, in aggregate and by type, all fees they receive from pharmaceutical manufacturers tied to patient utilization under a plan, and the amount and percentage passed through to the plan sponsor or issuer [S2].

Expands the reporting obligation to cover PBM affiliates under common ownership — including entities owned by the plans themselves — closing an obvious route to shift fee income to a sister company that would not otherwise have to report [S2].
Requires the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to publish an annual public report summarizing trends in the reported data, so the information would not sit in a federal filing cabinet [S2].

Takes effect for plan or contract years beginning on or after January 1, 2027, and lets the Secretary implement it by program instruction, exempting the paperwork from a federal review law that often delays new reporting rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their corporate affiliates would bear the cost of collecting and reporting fee data, and to the extent disclosure shows large margins retained rather than passed through, they would face pressure to give more of that money back to plans and consumers. Health plans would take on additional reporting of their own.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and health plans

drawbacks.text: Disclosure alone does not lower drug prices: the bill caps no fees, bans no spread pricing or reimbursement practices, and requires no money to be returned to consumers; PBMs that restructure or relabel fees could keep much of their revenue while technically complying [S2].

The bill reaches only Medicare drug plans, Medicare Advantage plans, and ACA marketplace plans, so the large employer-sponsored market — where most working-age people get drug coverage — is outside its reporting scope [S2].
Plans and PBMs would carry real administrative costs to disaggregate fees by type and track pass-through percentages, and those costs could ultimately show up in premiums [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: verified public data on what PBMs collect from manufacturers, broken down by type, is the foundation for any later crackdown on PBM pricing, and it would let plans and regulators see for the first time how much of the money flows back. But it is a first step, not a fix — nothing in the bill lowers a price or returns a dollar, and it skips the employer market where most working people get coverage. The administrative cost is small relative to the information gained, but the bill's narrow scope means its direct benefit to consumers would be indirect at best.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2024 and sent to two House committees, but it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress adjourned in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill in the House on March 19, 2024 [S1].

The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, a dual referral that means two committees would each have to act on the parts in their jurisdiction [S4].
Days later it went to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, with a further subcommittee referral recorded in December 2024; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded [S4].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor over the bill's lifetime [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills that do not pass both chambers die when a Congress ends; this one died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their corporate affiliates came out ahead, because they will not have to disclose manufacturer fees to Medicare, to health plans, or publicly; drugmakers that pay those fees also avoided the disclosure.

for.name: Rep. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter of record; it never advanced past subcommittee referral in his term.

against.name: House committees (Energy and Commerce; Ways and Means) and their leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from March 2024 through the end of the Congress without scheduling a hearing, a markup, or a vote; both committees were chaired by Republicans during the 118th Congress.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry
against.what_they_did: PBM companies including the three largest (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx) have broadly opposed disclosure mandates that would expose their manufacturer fee revenue; no direct action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill with no cosponsors of either party, and it never reached a vote, so the record shows no partisan split.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill targets PBMs directly: they and their affiliates would have to report every manufacturer fee they collect and how much is passed through to plans. The three biggest PBMs process most American prescriptions and earn much of their revenue from manufacturer fees and rebates, so verified public disclosure would directly expose their margins to regulators, plans, and the public.

Manufacturers pay the fees and rebates the bill would disclose, so disclosure could increase pressure on the PBM-manufacturer money flow and on list-price strategies built around rebates. But the bill imposes no direct requirement or cap on manufacturers themselves.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare/ACA plan sponsors
industries.note: Health benefits plans would take on a reporting duty of their own, but the same disclosure would hand plan sponsors hard data to negotiate against PBMs and potentially recover money retained rather than passed through.
